The finding

Can you tell whether a first-order logic formula says what its sentence says, with no gold formula and without reading the sentence at all?

Correct FOL is not unique, and benchmark gold is often wrong. The paper asks whether the other systems can serve as the reference. Nine current LLMs formalize the same sentence. An SMT solver checks which of their formulas are logically equivalent after a that never reads predicate names. A candidate's is the reliability-weighted share of peers equivalent to it.

On 450 fresh sentences, frozen before any label existed, the answer is yes for short benchmark text:

 
peer agreement ,
 
(gemini-2.5-flash), same items

Under the gap widens to 0.874 against 0.727. The gain it adds on top of a judge is small, though: about +0.03 AUROC on panel labels, with an interval that touches zero. It ties an existing estimator, and it falls below chance when most systems share an error.

Does peer agreement beat the judge under both label families, and on every corpus?

    Where it fails

    Agreement cannot see a mistake most peers make. The three views below show that boundary on fresh sentences, in a controlled dose test, and on long legal definitions.

    When the majority is wrong

    What happens to agreement on sentences whose is unfaithful?

    Panel items in sentences where the modal cluster is

    The modal cluster's correctness is read from the labels of its members (panel labels first, else solver labels), so this split is descriptive.

    The dose test

    How many peers must share a mistake before agreement prefers the mistake?

    200 development sentences, 560 items over four operators: k of the eight peers are replaced by renamed copies of a mutant. Detection is the probability that the faithful formula scores above the mutant.

    On real development data

    Concordance within sentences, by the share of peer weight held by clusters with the wrong meaning (6,772 faithful × unfaithful pairs in 508 sentences, development configuration).

    Long legal definitions

    Does agreement hold up on text rich in exceptions, where shared error is common?

    Weighted AUROC against panel labels from the sentence alone (no gold exists). These are the weakest labels in the study: Fleiss κ 0.38 overall and 0.17 on sentences with four or more markers.

    What the paper does not show

    • A clear increment. Added to a base of judge, roundtrip and structural scores, peer agreement gains +0.033 AUROC on panel labels, 95% CI [−0.001, 0.066]. It is significant only under a directional test, on 256 panel items (Kish effective sample size 202).
    • A gain over an existing estimator. It does not beat binary Dawid–Skene agreement on panel labels (−0.003), and its gain over majority clustering comes from reliability weighting.
    • Human labels. Panel labels are LLM judgments, with Cohen κ 0.57 against human corrections on MALLS. No human adjudication was used.
    • Every baseline as specified. Roundtrip baselines on the fresh and legal sets used a local Qwen3-8B back-translation, and the frontier judge was not run on fresh items. GenV, FormalAlign and the relabelling framework of Brunello et al. were not benchmarked.
    • Separation within a sentence. On development solver labels, shuffling labels within sentences leaves the score at 0.70 AUROC against a true 0.82, so much of its item-level AUROC separates easy sentences from hard ones.
    • Error types. No reference-free method in the study named real error types better than always predicting the most frequent type.
    • A lone output. The score needs several independent systems per sentence; with a system's own samples as peers it reduces to self-consistency (0.842 against 0.843).

    Where each view's data comes from

    • The finding, item browser, complexity, stepper, recompute, filter and shared-error views: experiment_3/method_out.json (4,050 fresh greedy candidates: scores, labels, panel weights, complexity features), joined with experiment_3/work/fresh_frame.jsonl (canonical formulas), experiment_3/results/scores.jsonl (roundtrip scores), experiment_3/work/fresh_dc_weights.json (Dawid–Skene weights) and the pairwise relations in experiment_3/work/pair_cache.jsonl, derived with the run's own dc.align.derive under the frozen configuration. Recomputing every candidate's score from those relations reproduces the recorded score for all 4,050 rows.
    • Confidence intervals on the unfiltered headline chart: experiment_3/results/tests.json.
    • Renaming test: experiment_4/results/m1_confound.json.
    • Dose test and real concordance: experiment_4/results/m3_boundary.json.
    • Legal definitions: experiment_5/method_out.json (655 panel-labelled candidates with sampling weights).

    AUROCs on panel labels are weighted by each item's sampling weight, as in the paper. Where a filter leaves only one label class, the view says so instead of drawing a value. No point is interpolated or smoothed.
